extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy, history, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how state institutions should manage religion and clergy power, and the social causes that strengthen or weaken ecclesiastical influence. Discusses remedies (education, public diversions), institutional arrangements (benefices, elections, papal collation), and historical effects of commerce and reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote study of science and philosophy among middling ranks
rubrics_metrics.description: The state might render the study of science and philosophy almost universal among all people of middling or more than middling rank and fortune by making learning a prerequisite for liberal professions and for candidates to honourable offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not achieve this by giving salaries to teachers (which makes them negligent and idle), but by instituting some sort of probation, even in higher sciences, that must be undergone before practicing a liberal profession or receiving office. The state need not provide teachers; those required to learn will find better teachers themselves. Science is the great antidote to enthusiasm and superstition; securing the superior ranks from superstition protects the inferior ranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage frequent and gay public diversions to dissipate superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: The state should encourage (by giving liberty) public amusements — painting, poetry, music, dancing, dramatic representations and exhibitions — to dissipate melancholy and gloomy humour that nourishes popular superstition and enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow those who can amuse the people without scandal or indecency. Dramatic representations are especially effective because they expose artifices to public ridicule and were historically objects of fanatical abhorrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial legal treatment of religions when no established church exists
rubrics_metrics.description: In a country where the law favours no one religion, teachers need not depend on the sovereign for appointment or removal; the sovereign's role is to keep the peace among religions, preventing persecution or oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign need only intervene to preserve public order; direct control of religious appointment is unnecessary and potentially harmful in such plural situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign must be able to influence clergy of an established church
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is an established or governing religion, the sovereign cannot be secure unless he can influence in considerable degree the greater part of the teachers of that religion because clergy, as an incorporated body, can act in concert and may have interests opposite to the sovereign's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clergy's authority depends on the supposed certainty and importance of doctrine; if clergy propagate doctrines subversive of sovereign authority, only violence or standing armies can maintain sovereign power — and these are precarious if soldiers are native and susceptible to clerical doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferment (rewards) over fear (punishment) to manage clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear is a wretched instrument of government, and attempting to terrify an order with pretensions to independence (like clergy) only irritates and confirms opposition; the sovereign should manage clergy by the preferment he can bestow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irregular violent deprivation of benefices makes clergy and doctrines more popular. Preferment (promotion, rewards) provides the means of influencing clergy more safely than punishment or force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid employing force against respected clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing force and violence against clergy tends to be the most dangerous and ruinous course: their rights and personal liberties are often more respected than other persons even under despotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management and persuasion are the easiest and safest instruments of government; force should be a last resort because it provokes stronger resistance and can make matters worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of the risks of transnational ecclesiastical control (papal collation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization of collation of benefices (as the pope did) creates a spiritual 'army' dispersed across countries whose operations can be directed by one head, making national sovereigns vulnerable to foreign ecclesiastical influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an arrangement can enable foreign spiritual authority to support clergy against native sovereigns and to turn clerical arms against a country's ruler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize how arts, manufactures, and commerce weaken clergy temporal power
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvements in arts, manufactures, and commerce destroyed the temporal power of the clergy in the same way they destroyed the power of great barons: clergy could exchange produce for manufactured goods and spend revenues on themselves, reducing charity and hospitality that previously secured popular allegiance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As charity and hospitality decline, clergy retainers and their influence dwindle; economic development undermines the material bases of clerical temporal power, leaving primarily spiritual authority which is also weakened when not supported by material ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore or secure sovereign influence through electoral and legal reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereigns sought to recover influence over church benefices by restoring ancient electoral rights (deans/chapters electing bishops, monks electing abbots) coupled with the sovereign's consent and approval, thereby gaining indirect means to influence clergy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-establishing election rights often required the sovereign's prior consent and later approval to render elections valid; such arrangements preserve a nominally free election while giving the sovereign indirect leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concordats and statutes to limit foreign ecclesiastical power
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal instruments like the statute of provisors and the pragmatic sanction, and later concordats, restrained papal power over collation of benefices and gave national sovereigns greater control over major ecclesiastical appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These agreements and statutes varied by country but could effectively limit papal interference (e.g., the concordat gave French kings the right of presentation to consistorial benefices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Episcopal (Lutheran/Anglican) church government favors civil order
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems preserving episcopal government, subordination among clergy, and sovereign disposal of bishoprics (as among Lutherans and the Church of England) render the sovereign the real head of the church and are favourable to peace, good order, and submission to civil authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under such systems clergy seek favour from the sovereign and elites, cultivate useful learning and decent manners, and generally avoid causing civil tumults; however, they may neglect influence among lower ranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parish election of pastors (Calvinist model) can produce fanaticism and disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: When each parish elects its own pastor, elections typically occur under clergy influence (often the most factious and fanatical) leading to fanatic candidates, factional contests, and disorder that can spill into civil schisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The people's right of election often led to clergy encouraging fanaticism to win parish elections; in small republics this could divide cities and threaten public peace, prompting magistrates to assume the right of presentation to preserve order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy neglect of lower ranks under court-oriented patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: A clergy that obtains preferment by courting sovereigns and elites tends to cultivate learning, manners, and loyalty to the upper ranks but is apt to neglect maintaining influence with lower ranks, making them vulnerable to popular fanatics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such clergy may be esteemed by superiors but ineffective at defending moderate doctrines before common people against ignorant enthusiasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fanatical sects gain social standing through strict austerity and mutual discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of small religious sects acquire consideration and regulate members' behaviour by enforcing austere morals and punishing scandal (expulsion/excommunication), which often results in more orderly morals among common people than in established churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the morals may be disagreeably rigorous or unsocial, sectarian internal discipline can make adherents appear respectable and control vice among their members.
